name: Security and Risk Management
plainMeaning: This domain is about how an organization decides what to protect, how much to spend, and who is responsible. It covers ethics, laws, policies, people and risk, which are the management foundations for all other security work.

topics.name: Professional ethics and the ISC2 Code
topics.simpleExplanation: Security people are trusted with secrets, money and the keys to important systems. So they must behave well. ISC2, the organization that runs the CISSP exam, has a code of ethics that every certified member must follow. It has four rules, called canons, and they come in a fixed order. Society comes first, then honest and legal behaviour, then your employer or client, then the profession. Your workplace will also have its own code of ethics. You must follow both, and you must help others follow them too.

studyNotes.heading: Why ethics matters in security
studyNotes.body:
Think of a locksmith. A locksmith can open any door in town. People only hire one they trust. A security professional is the same. You can often see private files, staff records and bank data.

Ethics means knowing what is right and doing it, even when nobody is watching. Being legal is not always enough. Something can be legal and still be wrong.

The ISC2 Code begins with a short opening statement called the preamble. It says that the safety and welfare of society and the common good, and our duty to the people we serve and to each other, require the highest standard of behaviour. It also says we must be seen to keep that standard. Looking honest matters as well as being honest.

studyNotes.heading: The four canons, in exact order
studyNotes.body:
A canon is a main rule. Learn these in order, because the order settles conflicts.

- Canon 1: Protect society, the common good, the public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
- Canon 2: Act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally.
- Canon 3: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
- Canon 4: Advance and protect the profession.

A principal is the person or organization you work for, such as your employer or client. Diligent means careful and hard-working. Competent means having the skill to do the job. Infrastructure means the big systems people depend on, like power, water and hospitals.

Canon 3 also means you should not accept work you are not qualified to do.

studyNotes.heading: When the canons clash
studyNotes.body:
Sometimes two canons pull in different directions. The higher canon wins.

Example: your client runs a dam. You find a flaw that could flood a town. The client asks you to say nothing. Your duty to the client is Canon 3. Your duty to the public is Canon 1. Canon 1 wins.

This does not mean you rush to social media. A good adviser raises the matter in writing with management, presses for a fix, and uses the proper legal route to tell the authorities if it is needed. Stay calm and follow the process. People's safety comes first.

studyNotes.heading: The organization's own code of ethics
studyNotes.body:
Most employers also have a code of ethics. It usually covers honest dealing, gifts, conflicts of interest and treatment of colleagues. A conflict of interest is when your private gain could affect your work decision.

Senior management should approve the code and follow it visibly. Staff should receive it, agree to it and be trained on it. Rules must be enforced fairly. As a security professional, you promote the code by your example.

studyNotes.heading: Complaints and consequences
studyNotes.body:
A member who breaks the ISC2 Code can face a formal complaint, and can lose the certification. Complaints go to ISC2 with supporting evidence. The person complaining must have been affected by the conduct.

Who may complain depends on the canon. Anyone in the public may complain under Canons 1 and 2. Only principals may complain under Canon 3. Only other professionals may complain under Canon 4.

keyTerms.meaning: The International Information System Security Certification Consortium: the organization that runs the CISSP certification.
Certified Information Systems Security Professional: the certification you are studying for.
A written set of rules about right and wrong behaviour.
One of the four main rules of the ISC2 Code.
The opening statement of the Code, which explains its purpose.
The employer or client you provide service to.
A situation where private gain could affect a work decision.

keyPoints: The four canons have a fixed order, and the higher canon wins a conflict.
Society and public safety come before your employer.
Do not accept work you are not competent to do.
You must follow both the ISC2 Code and your organization's code.
topics.memoryHook: Society, Honesty, Boss, Peers. Think of circles shrinking from the whole world down to your own profession.

question.prompt: A security consultant working for a water company finds a flaw that could let attackers change the chemical levels in drinking water. The company's manager tells the consultant to leave it out of the report to avoid bad publicity. What should the consultant do?
options: Leave it out of the report, because the duty to the client who pays for the work comes first
Publish the details online so the public can protect itself straight away
Escalate it in writing and press for a fix, using proper legal routes if needed
Fix the control system quietly without telling anyone at the company
question.explanation: Public safety under Canon 1 ranks above duty to a client under Canon 3, so silence is wrong. Publishing is tempting, but it arms attackers and is not responsible behaviour. The proper route protects the public and stays honest and legal.

topics.name: Core security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, nonrepudiation
topics.simpleExplanation: Almost all of security aims at five goals. Confidentiality keeps secrets from the wrong people. Integrity keeps information correct and unchanged. Availability makes sure things work when people need them. Authenticity means something is genuine, and really comes from who it claims. Nonrepudiation means a person cannot later deny they did something. Think of a signed letter in a sealed envelope, delivered on time. Every control you study later supports at least one of these goals. When you read an exam question, ask which goal is at risk.

studyNotes.heading: The CIA triad
studyNotes.body:
CIA here stands for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability. It has nothing to do with spies. A triad is a group of three.

Confidentiality means only allowed people can see the information. Your bank balance should be seen by you and the bank, not your neighbour. Tools include encryption, access control and data classification. Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Threats include stolen laptops, eavesdropping and shoulder surfing, which is reading over someone's shoulder.

Integrity means information stays correct and is only changed by allowed people in allowed ways. If a school's exam mark changes from 40 to 90 without permission, integrity has failed. Tools include hashing, digital signatures, change control and input checks. A hash is a short fingerprint of data. If the data changes, the fingerprint changes.

Availability means systems and data are there when needed. A cash machine that is always broken has an availability problem. Tools include backups, spare equipment, spare power and protection against denial of service attacks. These attacks flood a system so real users cannot get in.

studyNotes.heading: Authenticity and nonrepudiation
studyNotes.body:
Authenticity means something is genuine. An email that truly came from your bank is authentic. A fake one is not.

Do not confuse this with authentication. Authentication is the act of proving who you are, such as entering a password. Authenticity is the quality of being genuine.

Nonrepudiation means a person cannot successfully deny an action. To repudiate means to deny. Your signature on a contract gives this in the paper world.

In the digital world, the main tool is a digital signature made with a private key that only one person holds. It gives integrity, authenticity and nonrepudiation. It does not give confidentiality, because anyone may still read a signed message.

A key shared by two people cannot give nonrepudiation, because either person could have used it. Shared user accounts fail for the same reason. Good logs tied to individual users support nonrepudiation.

studyNotes.heading: The opposite: DAD
studyNotes.body:
DAD lists what attackers try to cause.

- Disclosure attacks confidentiality.
- Alteration attacks integrity.
- Destruction, or denial, attacks availability.

studyNotes.heading: Balancing the goals
studyNotes.body:
You cannot maximize everything at once. Very strong locks may slow down real work. A hospital must protect patient records, but a doctor must also reach them in an emergency.

The right balance depends on what the business does. A newspaper website values availability and integrity, and its articles are public. A military plan values confidentiality most.

Think like an adviser. Ask what the organization needs, then choose controls that fit. When lives are at stake, safety decides.

keyTerms.meaning: Only allowed people can see the information.
Information stays correct and is changed only in allowed ways.
Systems and data are ready when needed.
Something is genuine and comes from who it claims.
A person cannot successfully deny having done something.
A short fingerprint of data that changes if the data changes.
A check made with a private key that proves who signed and that nothing changed.
Disclosure, Alteration and Destruction: the opposites of the CIA triad.

keyPoints: CIA stands for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
A digital signature gives integrity, authenticity and nonrepudiation, but not confidentiality.
Shared keys and shared accounts cannot prove which person acted.
The right balance of goals depends on the needs of the business.
topics.memoryHook: A signed letter in a sealed envelope, delivered on time: sealed is confidential, untouched is integrity, on time is availability, the real sender is authentic, and the signature means no denying it.

question.prompt: A company has a dispute with a manager who says she never approved a large payment. The company wants to stop this kind of dispute in future. Which control would BEST meet this need?
options: Encrypting all payment files while they are stored on the server
Having each approver sign payments with a personal private key
Keeping an approval log for one shared finance team account
Calculating a hash of every payment file each night
question.explanation: The need is nonrepudiation, and a personal private key ties the approval to one person. A log is tempting, but a shared account cannot show who acted. Encryption gives secrecy, and a hash only shows whether a file changed.

topics.name: Security governance principles
topics.simpleExplanation: Governance means how leaders direct and oversee an organization. Security governance makes sure security helps the business reach its goals. Security must also fit changes such as buying or selling a company. Everyone needs a clear role, and the top leaders stay responsible. Many organizations follow a published control framework, which is a ready-made guide to good security. Two ideas are tested often. Due diligence is researching, planning and checking. Due care is doing the right thing in practice. A wise leader does both.

studyNotes.heading: Alignment to the business
studyNotes.body:
Security exists to support the business, not the other way round. A security plan should fit the strategy, goals, mission and objectives of the organization.

A small school and a large bank need different security. Good security leaders learn what the business wants first.

Governance works from the top down. Senior leaders set direction and provide money and people. Without their support, a security program fails.

Plans come in three levels:

- Strategic: long-term, often about five years.
- Tactical: mid-term, often about a year.
- Operational: short-term and detailed, such as this month's tasks.

studyNotes.heading: Organizational processes
studyNotes.body:
Some business events change risk quickly.

An acquisition is when one company buys another. Check the other company's security before joining networks, or you may inherit its problems.

A divestiture is when part of a company is sold or closed. Remove access for staff who leave, and clean or transfer data and equipment correctly.

A governance committee is a group of leaders from different departments who review security decisions and priorities. This gives security support across the business.

studyNotes.heading: Roles and responsibilities
studyNotes.body:
- Senior management: ultimately responsible for security. They can give out tasks, but not their final responsibility.
- Chief Information Security Officer (CISO): leads the security program and advises leaders.
- Security professionals: design and run controls.
- Data owner: a manager accountable for a set of data, who decides its classification.
- Data custodian: carries out the daily care of data, such as backups.
- Users: follow policy.
- Auditors: check independently that controls work and report to management.

studyNotes.heading: Control frameworks
studyNotes.body:
A control framework is an organized set of security practices. Know what each one is for.

- ISO 27001: an international standard from the International Organization for Standardization for an information security management system. An organization can be certified against it.
- ISO 27002: guidance on the controls.
- NIST: the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. SP 800-53 is its control catalogue. Its Cybersecurity Framework has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- COBIT: Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology, for governing and managing company technology.
- SABSA: Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture, which builds security design from business needs.
- PCI DSS: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, for anyone handling payment cards.
- FedRAMP: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program, for cloud services used by the US government.

studyNotes.heading: Due care and due diligence
studyNotes.body:
Imagine a landlord. Finding out what the fire code demands, planning for it and checking the alarms each month is due diligence. Actually installing the alarms and repairing the broken stair is due care.

Due diligence is the research, planning and checking. Due care is taking the reasonable action. If leaders fail at either one, they can be found negligent, which means legally at fault for not being careful enough.

keyTerms.meaning: How leaders direct, control and oversee an organization.
One company buying another.
Selling or closing part of a company.
Chief Information Security Officer: the leader of the security program.
An organized, published set of security practices.
Researching, planning and checking what should be done.
Taking the reasonable action to protect people and assets.
Being legally at fault for failing to take reasonable care.

keyPoints: Security must support the goals of the business.
Senior management holds final responsibility and cannot hand it away.
Check a company's security before connecting to it in an acquisition.
Due diligence is planning and checking, and due care is doing.
topics.memoryHook: Diligence is the Detective who studies and checks. Care is the Carpenter who fixes the stair.

question.prompt: A retail company is about to buy a smaller online shop. The technology team wants to connect the two networks next week so that staff can share systems. What should the security manager recommend FIRST?
options: Connect the networks now, then scan the smaller shop's systems afterwards
Ask the shop's staff to change all their passwords on the day of connection
Install a firewall between the networks and allow all traffic for the first month
Assess the smaller shop's security and risks before any connection is made
question.explanation: In an acquisition you can inherit the other company's weaknesses, so assessment comes first. This is due diligence. Scanning afterwards is tempting, but by then any existing compromise could already have spread across the networks.

topics.name: Compliance, laws and regulations
topics.simpleExplanation: Compliance means obeying the rules that apply to you. Some rules are laws. Others come from regulators, industry bodies or contracts you signed. Security staff must know which rules apply. Privacy laws protect personal information. Intellectual property law protects ideas and creative work. Other laws control which technologies may leave a country, and where data may travel. Cybercrime and data breaches bring their own duties, including telling people when data is exposed. A security professional is not a lawyer, so always involve legal advisers when the law is unclear.

studyNotes.heading: Where requirements come from
studyNotes.body:
- Legal: laws made by government. Breaking them can bring fines or prison.
- Regulatory: rules from a government agency that oversees an area, such as banking.
- Industry standards: rules set by an industry. The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) applies to anyone handling payment cards. It is not a law. Card companies enforce it through contracts.
- Contractual: promises in an agreement. Break them and the other party may sue.

The company must list which of these apply and review the list often.

studyNotes.heading: Privacy
studyNotes.body:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is any data that can identify a person, such as a name with a birth date.

The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) protects people in the EU, even when the company is elsewhere. Key facts:

- A data subject is the person the data is about.
- A controller decides why and how data is used.
- A processor handles data on the controller's behalf.
- A breach must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to harm people.
- The highest fines reach 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide yearly turnover, whichever is higher.

Other laws to recognize:

- California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA).
- Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) in China.
- Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) in South Africa.
- Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) for US health data.
- Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) for US financial customer data.
- Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) for accurate financial reporting by US public companies.

studyNotes.heading: Intellectual property and licensing
studyNotes.body:
Intellectual property means things created by the mind.

- Copyright: protects creative works, including software code. Often lasts the author's life plus 70 years.
- Trademark: protects names and logos. It can be renewed without limit.
- Patent: protects inventions, usually for 20 years from filing. The details become public.
- Trade secret: protects valuable secret business information, such as a recipe. It lasts as long as it stays secret.

A licence is permission to use software. Common forms are signed contracts, shrink-wrap, click-through and cloud service terms. Track licences, because using more copies than you paid for is a violation.

studyNotes.heading: Moving technology and data across borders
studyNotes.body:
Import and export controls limit which goods can cross borders. In the US, the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) cover military items. The Export Administration Regulations (EAR) cover commercial and dual-use items, including some encryption. Dual-use means useful for both civilian and military purposes.

Transborder data flow means personal data moving between countries. Some countries require data to stay inside their borders. GDPR allows transfers to countries it judges to have adequate protection, or with safeguards such as standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules.

studyNotes.heading: Cybercrime and data breaches
studyNotes.body:
Cybercrime includes hacking, fraud and stealing data. Attackers often sit in another country, which makes jurisdiction hard. Jurisdiction means which country's law and courts apply.

After a breach, follow your plan. Involve legal advisers early. Notify authorities and affected people as the law requires.

keyTerms.meaning: Meeting the rules that apply to the organization.
Personally Identifiable Information: data that can identify a person.
General Data Protection Regulation: the European Union's main privacy law.
The party that decides why and how personal data is used.
The party that handles personal data for the controller.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: an industry rule set for card data, enforced by contract.
Valuable business information protected for as long as it stays secret.
Moving data across national borders.
Which country's law and courts apply.

keyPoints: PCI DSS is an industry standard enforced by contract, not a law.
GDPR breach reports are due within 72 hours of becoming aware.
A trade secret lasts only as long as it stays secret.
Check where data will travel before sending it across a border.
Involve legal advisers when the law is unclear.
topics.memoryHook: Copyright for Creations, Trademark for Tags, Patents for Parts that are new, Secrets for the Sauce.

question.prompt: An online shop that sells to customers in Germany confirms on Monday morning that attackers copied customer names and home addresses, and the breach is likely to harm those customers. Under GDPR, what is the shop's deadline to notify the supervisory authority?
options: Within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach
Within 30 days, once the full investigation has ended
Within 24 hours of the moment the attackers first got in
Only after law enforcement has given its written agreement
question.explanation: GDPR sets 72 hours from becoming aware of the breach. Waiting for the investigation to end is tempting, but GDPR expects a report on time, and further details can follow in stages.

topics.name: Types of investigation
topics.simpleExplanation: When something goes wrong, someone investigates. There are five types to know. Administrative investigations are internal matters inside the organization. Criminal investigations involve police and possible punishment. Civil cases are disputes between parties, often over money. Regulatory investigations are run by a government agency that oversees an area of work. Industry standards investigations check whether an organization met the rules of its industry. Each type needs a different amount of proof. An internal case can turn into a criminal one, so always protect the evidence from the start.

studyNotes.heading: Why the type matters
studyNotes.body:
The type of investigation decides who leads it, how evidence is handled, and how much proof is needed. The amount of proof needed is called the standard of proof or burden of proof.

Think of a school. A teacher looking into a broken window has a lighter task than a court trying someone for arson. The result of the court case is far more serious, so it needs stronger proof.

studyNotes.heading: The five types
studyNotes.body:
Administrative

- Run inside the organization, often by human resources or the security team.
- Looks at operational problems and staff behaviour, such as misuse of email.
- Lowest standard of proof. The aim is usually to find the cause and solve the problem.

Criminal

- Run by law enforcement, such as the police, for suspected crimes.
- The standard is beyond a reasonable doubt. This is the highest standard.
- Can lead to prison or fines. Evidence rules are very strict.

Civil

- A dispute between two parties, such as a company and a supplier over a contract.
- The standard is preponderance of the evidence, which means more likely than not. Think of it as just over 50 percent.
- Usually leads to payment of money, not prison.

Regulatory

- Run by a government regulator, or by people working for it, to check whether regulations were broken.
- The standard varies with the regulator and the rule involved.
- Can lead to fines and orders to change.

Industry standards

- Checks compliance with rules set by an industry, such as the card payment industry's standard.
- Often done by an outside assessor, and shaped by the contract.
- Can lead to penalties, higher fees or loss of the right to take card payments.

studyNotes.heading: Protecting evidence
studyNotes.body:
Evidence must be collected so that it can be trusted later. Chain of custody is the written record of who held the evidence, when, and what they did with it. If the record has gaps, a court may not trust the evidence.

An administrative investigation can quickly become something bigger. Suppose you are looking into an employee who wastes time online, and you find proof of theft from customers. It is now possibly a crime. Handle every case from the start as if it could reach a court.

studyNotes.heading: What a manager should do
studyNotes.body:
Follow the organization's incident and investigation procedure. It should be agreed before anything goes wrong.

Before going to the police, consult senior management and legal advisers. Calling law enforcement may make the case public and may mean losing control of it.

Do not delete anything, and do not confront the suspect on your own. If you suspect a serious crime, stop, keep what you found safe, and contact legal advisers. Respect privacy and follow the law while you gather facts.

keyTerms.meaning: An internal inquiry into operations or staff behaviour.
An inquiry by law enforcement into a suspected crime.
A dispute between parties, usually over money or a contract.
An inquiry by a government oversight body or for it.
The highest standard of proof, used in criminal cases.
More likely than not. The standard used in civil cases.
A written record of who held evidence, when, and what they did.

keyPoints: Criminal cases need proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Civil cases need only a preponderance of the evidence.
Administrative cases have the lowest standard of proof.
Any internal case could become criminal, so protect evidence from the start.
topics.memoryHook: Criminal is Certain, Civil is Coin-flip-plus. Prison needs far more proof than payment.

question.prompt: A company takes a former supplier to court to recover money it lost when the supplier broke a contract. The court will not consider sending anyone to prison. What standard of proof is the company MOST likely required to meet?
options: Beyond a reasonable doubt
Proof to absolute certainty
Preponderance of the evidence
Whatever the human resources policy states
question.explanation: A contract dispute between two parties is a civil case, so the standard is more likely than not. Beyond a reasonable doubt sounds strong and is tempting, but it applies to criminal cases.

topics.name: Policies, standards, procedures, guidelines, baselines
topics.simpleExplanation: Organizations write security rules in layers. A policy is the top-level statement from leaders about what must be achieved. A standard says which specific tools or settings everyone must use. A baseline sets the minimum security level for a type of system. A guideline gives helpful advice that you may choose to follow. A procedure gives exact steps for doing a task. Everything is mandatory except guidelines. Think of a school: the rule, the uniform, the minimum dress code, the helpful tips, and the steps for fire drills.

studyNotes.heading: The five documents
studyNotes.body:
Policy

- High level. Says what the organization wants and why.
- Approved by senior management, which gives it authority.
- Mandatory.
- Does not name products. Example: 'Customer data must be protected wherever it is stored.'

Standard

- Says what specific technology, method or level must be used.
- Mandatory. Example: 'All company laptops must use the approved full-disk encryption product.'

Baseline

- The minimum security settings for a type of system.
- Mandatory. Example: a list of settings every new web server must start with.

Guideline

- Advice and recommended good practice.
- Optional. It is the only one of the five that is not mandatory. Example: 'Consider using a phrase for your password, so that it is easy to remember.'

Procedure

- Exact step-by-step instructions for one task.
- Mandatory. Example: step 1, plug in the laptop; step 2, open the encryption tool; step 3, record the recovery key.

studyNotes.heading: How they fit together
studyNotes.body:
Think of the order from general to specific: policy, standards, baselines, guidelines, procedures.

Each layer supports the one above it. A standard exists to carry out a policy. A procedure explains how to meet a standard. If they conflict, the higher document wins and the lower one should be corrected.

Here is a worked example from a bank:

- Policy: Only allowed staff may reach customer accounts.
- Standard: Everyone must use multi-factor authentication, which means proving who you are in at least two different ways, such as a password and a phone code.
- Baseline: Every staff computer locks after ten minutes.
- Guideline: Keep your phone close so codes arrive quickly.
- Procedure: Steps the help desk follows to set up a new user's phone.

studyNotes.heading: Kinds of policy
studyNotes.body:
- Organizational policy: the overall security program and its purpose.
- Issue-specific policy: one topic, such as email use or remote working. An acceptable use policy is a common example. It tells staff what they may and may not do with company systems.
- System-specific policy: the rules for one system.

Policies can also be described by purpose:

- Regulatory: needed by law or regulation.
- Advisory: tells staff what behaviour is expected and what happens if they break the rule.
- Informative: gives information only, with no enforcement.

studyNotes.heading: Keeping them alive
studyNotes.body:
Policies only work if people know them, understand them and face fair consequences for ignoring them. Staff should read and accept the policy. Documents need regular review, and also after big changes in the law, business or technology.

Policies should stay fairly stable because they do not name products. When technology changes, you can change a standard or a procedure without going back to the board.

keyTerms.meaning: A mandatory, high-level statement from senior management.
A mandatory rule on the specific technology or level to use.
The mandatory minimum security settings for a type of system.
Optional advice and recommended practice.
Mandatory step-by-step instructions for one task.
A policy that says what staff may and may not do with company systems.
Proving who you are in at least two different ways.

keyPoints: Guidelines are the only optional document of the five.
Policies are approved by senior management and do not name products.
Procedures give exact step-by-step instructions.
A lower document must support the one above it.
topics.memoryHook: Policy says Why, Standard says Which, Baseline says the Bare minimum, Guideline says Go on if you like, Procedure says Press this next.

question.prompt: A security analyst is drafting a document that applies to all staff. It states that every company laptop must use one specific approved disk encryption product. It does not give setup steps or say why the organization protects data. Which type of document is this?
options: A policy
A standard
A guideline
A procedure
question.explanation: It is mandatory and names a specific technology, so it is a standard. A policy is tempting because it is also mandatory, but a policy stays high level and does not name products.

topics.name: Business continuity requirements and business impact analysis, with RTO, RPO, MTD
topics.simpleExplanation: Business continuity means keeping the most important work going during a disaster, such as a flood, fire or major outage. First you do a business impact analysis. It finds which activities matter most and how much harm a stoppage would cause. It gives three key measures. Maximum Tolerable Downtime is the longest the business can survive without an activity. Recovery Time Objective is the target time to restore it. Recovery Point Objective is how much recent data you can afford to lose. People's safety always comes first.

studyNotes.heading: Business continuity basics
studyNotes.body:
Business continuity planning (BCP) prepares the whole organization to keep working during and after a disruption. Disaster recovery focuses on restoring the technology and is covered later in the course.

The usual order of work is:

- Project scope and planning. Get senior management support, name the team and agree the budget.
- Business impact analysis.
- Continuity planning. Decide strategies and arrangements.
- Plan approval and implementation, including training.

Senior management must support and approve the plan. The team should include people from every key department, not only the technology team.

studyNotes.heading: Business impact analysis
studyNotes.body:
A business impact analysis (BIA) finds what would hurt most if it stopped. It looks at impact only. It does not choose solutions yet.

Steps:

- List the business activities and the people and systems they need.
- Decide how critical each activity is.
- Estimate the harm from stoppage over time.
- Set recovery priorities and time limits.

Impact can be quantitative, meaning measured in numbers such as lost money. It can also be qualitative, meaning described in words, such as lost trust, harm to reputation or danger to people. Both matter.

studyNotes.heading: RTO, RPO and MTD
studyNotes.body:
Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) is the longest an activity can be down before the organization suffers serious, possibly fatal, harm. You may also see it called maximum tolerable period of disruption.

Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the target time to bring the system back after a disruption. RTO must be shorter than MTD.

Work Recovery Time (WRT) is the extra time to test the restored system and get data up to date before real work continues.

The rule is: RTO + WRT must not be more than MTD.

Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the most data you can afford to lose, measured in time. It looks backwards from the disaster. Backups must run at least as often as the RPO.

studyNotes.heading: Worked example
studyNotes.body:
A shop's online order system has been studied.

- MTD is 8 hours.
- Testing and catching up on orders takes 2 hours, so WRT is 2 hours.
- Longest allowed RTO is 8 - 2 = 6 hours.
- The business can afford to lose 15 minutes of orders, so RPO is 15 minutes.
- Backups or data copies must happen at least every 15 minutes.

If a nightly backup is all the shop has, it could lose up to 24 hours of orders, and the RPO is not met.

Shorter times usually cost more, so the business must balance cost against harm.

studyNotes.heading: External dependencies
studyNotes.body: No business works alone. A plan must also consider what you rely on from outside: electricity, internet providers, cloud services, suppliers and delivery firms. Ask what happens if each one fails. Look for a single point of failure, which is one thing whose failure stops everything. Check that your supplier's recovery times meet your own.

keyTerms.meaning: Business Continuity Planning: preparing to keep working during a disruption.
Business Impact Analysis: finding which activities matter most and the harm if they stop.
Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest an activity can be down before serious harm.
Recovery Time Objective: the target time to bring a system back.
Recovery Point Objective: the most data you can afford to lose, measured in time.
Work Recovery Time: time to test and catch up before normal work continues.
One item whose failure stops the whole activity.

keyPoints: Get senior management support before anything else.
A BIA measures impact and does not choose solutions.
RTO + WRT must not be more than MTD.
RPO is about lost data and looks backwards from the disaster.
People's safety always comes first.
topics.memoryHook: RTO is the clock forward to get running. RPO is the clock backward to the last good copy. MTD is the cliff edge.

question.prompt: A clinic has set a Recovery Point Objective of one hour for its patient records. The records are currently backed up once each night. A review has just compared these two facts. What is the BEST conclusion?
options: The arrangement is fine, because the system can be restored within one hour
The Maximum Tolerable Downtime must be increased to 24 hours
The Recovery Time Objective should be reduced to under one hour
The requirement is not met, because the clinic could lose nearly a full day of records
question.explanation: RPO limits lost data, so copies must be made at least hourly. A nightly backup could lose almost 24 hours. Reducing the RTO is tempting, but RTO measures restore time and does nothing about how old the backup is.

topics.name: Personnel security
topics.simpleExplanation: People can be a company's strongest defence or its greatest weakness. Personnel security manages the risk from staff across their whole time with the company. You check people before hiring, have them sign agreements, and give them only the access they need. When people change jobs, old access must be removed. When they leave, access must end promptly. Vendors and contractors need similar rules. Staff must follow policy and face fair consequences if they do not. Their privacy must also be respected, including telling them about any monitoring.

studyNotes.heading: Screening and hiring
studyNotes.body:
Security starts with the job description. It should state the duties, the access needed and the required trust level.

Candidate screening means checking a person before hiring. Common checks are references, education, past employment, criminal record and sometimes credit history. The check should match the risk of the job. Checks must follow local law and treat people fairly. Often the candidate must give permission first.

Think of a bank hiring a cashier. It checks their past first, because they will handle money.

studyNotes.heading: Agreements and everyday controls
studyNotes.body:
New staff sign agreements. An employment agreement sets out duties and rules. A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) is a promise to keep information secret, often even after leaving. An acceptable use policy says how company systems may be used.

Helpful everyday controls are:

- Least privilege: give only the access needed for the job.
- Separation of duties: split a sensitive task between people, so one person cannot commit fraud alone. Collusion is when people secretly work together to get around this.
- Job rotation: moving staff through roles, which helps discover fraud and builds backup skills.
- Mandatory vacation: requiring time off, so that someone else does the work and may notice wrongdoing.

studyNotes.heading: Onboarding, transfers and termination
studyNotes.body:
Onboarding means bringing a new person in. They receive accounts with least privilege, security training and a copy of the policies.

A transfer means moving to a new role. Remove old access and add only what the new role needs. If you only ever add access, you get privilege creep, which is the slow build-up of too much access.

Termination means the end of employment. It may be voluntary or forced. For a forced termination:

- Disable all access at the same moment the person is told, or just before.
- Hold the meeting with a manager and a witness, usually from human resources.
- Collect badges, keys and devices.
- Escort the person from the building.
- Hold an exit interview where possible, and remind them of the agreements they signed.
- Check accounts afterwards and keep records as required.

Be respectful. Protect people's safety and dignity.

studyNotes.heading: Vendors, consultants and contractors
studyNotes.body: Outsiders can have real access to your systems, so treat them with the same care. Use written agreements that cover NDAs, security duties, access limits and the right to audit. Review their access regularly and end it when the work ends. Your organization stays responsible for its data, even when someone else handles it.

studyNotes.heading: Policy compliance and privacy
studyNotes.body:
Policy compliance means staff actually follow the rules. Train them, ask them to acknowledge the policy, monitor behaviour and apply fair, consistent consequences. Managers must follow the rules too.

Employees also have privacy rights. Tell staff in advance if email, internet use or systems are monitored, for example through a policy and login banner. Collect only the personal data the job needs, and keep it protected.

keyTerms.meaning: Checking a person's background before hiring.
Non-Disclosure Agreement: a promise to keep information secret.
Giving only the access needed for the job.
Splitting a sensitive task so one person cannot complete it alone.
People secretly working together to get around a control.
Moving staff through roles to find fraud and build backup skills.
Required time off, so someone else can see the person's work.
Slow build-up of too much access as a person changes roles.

keyPoints: Match screening to the risk of the job, and follow the law.
On a transfer, remove old access before or as you add new access.
For a forced termination, disable access when the person is told.
Tell staff in advance if they are monitored.
topics.memoryHook: Hire with a check, work with a limit, move with a clean-up, leave with a lockout.

question.prompt: An employee who worked in accounts has moved to the marketing team. An access review six months later shows she can still approve payments and also has every marketing permission. What is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Change the transfer process to remove old access at every role change
Remove her payment access and remind her not to use it again
Run a yearly report that lists all staff who changed departments during the year
Move her to a role where the payment access would be useful
question.explanation: This is privilege creep caused by a weak process, so the process must be fixed. Removing her access is tempting and should also happen, but it fixes only one person and not the cause.

topics.name: Risk management
topics.simpleExplanation: Risk is the chance that something bad will happen and the harm it would cause. Risk management means finding those risks, measuring them and deciding what to do. You can measure risk in words or in money. Then management chooses to reduce it, transfer it, avoid it or accept it. Controls are the safeguards used to reduce risk. They must be checked and monitored over time. Security staff advise, but senior management makes the final decision about how much risk to accept.

studyNotes.heading: Basic words
studyNotes.body:
- Asset: anything of value.
- Threat: something that could cause harm, such as a thief or a flood.
- Vulnerability: a weakness, such as a broken lock.
- Risk: the chance a threat uses a weakness, and the harm that results.
- Exposure: being open to possible loss.
- Safeguard or control: something that reduces risk.

Risk analysis can be qualitative, using words like high or low, often in a risk matrix. The Delphi method gathers anonymous expert opinions. Quantitative analysis uses money and numbers. Scope means deciding what the assessment covers.

studyNotes.heading: The math, with a worked example
studyNotes.body:
- Asset Value (AV): what the asset is worth.
- Exposure Factor (EF): percent lost in one event.
- Single Loss Expectancy: SLE = AV x EF.
- Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO): times per year.
- Annualized Loss Expectancy: ALE = SLE x ARO.

A warehouse is worth $500,000. A flood would destroy 40 percent. A flood is expected once in 10 years.

- SLE = $500,000 x 0.40 = $200,000.
- ARO = 1 / 10 = 0.1.
- ALE = $200,000 x 0.1 = $20,000 per year.

A barrier costs $8,000 a year and lowers ALE to $5,000. Safeguard value = (ALE before - ALE after) - yearly cost. So ($20,000 - $5,000) - $8,000 = $7,000. A positive result means it is worth buying.

studyNotes.heading: Risk response
studyNotes.body:
- Mitigate: reduce the risk with controls.
- Transfer or share: pass the cost to another party, such as through cybersecurity insurance. Accountability stays with you.
- Avoid: stop the risky activity.
- Accept: knowingly live with it, with management's written approval.

Ignoring a risk is never acceptable. Inherent risk exists before controls. Residual risk remains after them. Senior management decides what residual risk to accept.

studyNotes.heading: Control types
studyNotes.body:
Controls are grouped by how they work: administrative (policies), technical or logical (firewalls), and physical (fences).

They are also grouped by purpose:

- Preventive: stops an event. A lock.
- Detective: discovers an event. A camera recording.
- Corrective: fixes things after an event. Removing a virus.
- Deterrent: discourages. A warning sign.
- Recovery: restores operations. Backups.
- Compensating: an alternative when the main control cannot be used.
- Directive: tells people what to do. A policy.

studyNotes.heading: Assessing, monitoring and improving
studyNotes.body:
Control assessments test whether security and privacy controls really work. Continuous monitoring and measurement watch risk over time. Results are reported internally to leaders and externally to regulators, customers or auditors as required.

A risk maturity model shows how well an organization manages risk. One common order is ad hoc, preliminary, defined, integrated, optimized.

studyNotes.heading: Risk frameworks
studyNotes.body:
The NIST Risk Management Framework, from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, has seven steps in order: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

Others include ISO 31000 and ISO 27005 (international standards), COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology), SABSA (Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture), PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) and FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk), which measures risk in money.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that could cause harm.
A weakness that a threat could use.
Single Loss Expectancy: the money lost in one event. AV x EF.
Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.
Annualized Loss Expectancy: expected loss per year. SLE x ARO.
The risk that remains after controls are in place.
The risk that exists before any controls are added.
Passing the cost of a risk to another party, such as an insurer.
An alternative control used when the main one cannot be used.

keyPoints: SLE = AV x EF, and ALE = SLE x ARO.
The four responses are mitigate, transfer, avoid and accept.
Ignoring a risk is never a valid response.
Senior management decides how much residual risk to accept.
topics.memoryHook: AV times EF gives one hit (SLE). One hit times how often gives the yearly bill (ALE).

question.prompt: After new controls were added, a security manager reports that some risk to the customer database still remains and that further controls would cost more than the possible loss. Who should make the final decision to accept this remaining risk?
options: The security manager who carried out the assessment
The database administrators who look after the system every day
Senior management, with the decision formally recorded
The external auditor who reviews the database each year
question.explanation: Senior management is accountable and decides what residual risk to accept. The security manager is the tempting choice, but that role advises and does not own the business decision.

topics.name: Threat modeling
topics.simpleExplanation: Threat modeling means thinking like an attacker before an attack happens. You study a system, ask what could go wrong, and plan defences while changes are still cheap. Imagine walking around your house, noticing every door and window a burglar could use. Several methods help. STRIDE gives a list of threat types. PASTA is a seven-stage process tied to business risk. DREAD gives threats a score, so you can fix the worst first. The best time to begin is early, at the design stage.

studyNotes.heading: What threat modeling does
studyNotes.body:
A threat is anything that could cause harm. Threat modeling is a structured way to find threats and decide what to do about them.

It can be proactive, which means done during design, before problems exist. It can be reactive, which means done on a finished system. Proactive is cheaper and better.

You can begin your thinking from different starting points:

- Assets: what are we protecting?
- Attackers: who might attack us, and why?
- Software: where is the system itself weak?

Common steps:

- Identify the assets and the goals.
- Draw how the system works, often as a data flow diagram.
- Identify the threats.
- Rate them.
- Decide on responses and record them.

When breaking down a system, look at trust boundaries, data flow paths, input points, privileged operations and the security approach used. A trust boundary is a line where the level of trust changes, such as between the internet and your internal network.

studyNotes.heading: STRIDE
studyNotes.body:
STRIDE came from Microsoft. Each letter is a type of threat, and each one breaks a security goal.

- Spoofing: pretending to be someone else. Breaks authenticity.
- Tampering: changing data without permission. Breaks integrity.
- Repudiation: denying an action. Breaks nonrepudiation.
- Information disclosure: exposing data. Breaks confidentiality.
- Denial of service: stopping access for real users. Breaks availability.
- Elevation of privilege: gaining more power than allowed. Breaks authorization, which is the control over what you may do.

studyNotes.heading: PASTA
studyNotes.body:
PASTA means Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis. It is risk-centric, which means it connects threats to business impact. It has seven stages, in this order:

- 1. Definition of objectives.
- 2. Definition of technical scope.
- 3. Application decomposition and analysis.
- 4. Threat analysis.
- 5. Weakness and vulnerability analysis.
- 6. Attack modeling and simulation.
- 7. Risk analysis and management.

studyNotes.heading: DREAD
studyNotes.body:
DREAD gives a score to each threat, so you can rank them. Each letter is a question.

- Damage: how bad would it be?
- Reproducibility: how easily can it be repeated?
- Exploitability: how easily can the attack be carried out?
- Affected users: how many people are hit?
- Discoverability: how easily can it be found?

Example: rate each item from 1 to 10. A threat scoring 8, 9, 7, 10 and 6 totals 40 out of 50, so it is high priority.

studyNotes.heading: Other methods
studyNotes.body:
- VAST (Visual, Agile, Simple Threat): designed to fit agile development at large scale.
- Trike: focuses on risk and on what each person is allowed to do with each asset.
- Attack trees: a diagram with the attacker's goal at the top and the ways to reach it as branches.

Threat modeling is not a one-time job. Repeat it when the system changes.

keyTerms.meaning: A structured way of finding threats to a system and planning responses.
Done early, before a problem happens.
A line where the level of trust changes.
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis: a seven-stage, risk-centric method.
Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability: a scoring method.
Visual, Agile, Simple Threat: a method built for agile development at scale.
A diagram showing an attacker's goal and the ways to reach it.

keyPoints: Start threat modeling early, during design.
STRIDE classifies threats, and DREAD scores them.
PASTA has seven stages and ties threats to business risk.
Repeat threat modeling whenever the system changes.
topics.memoryHook: STRIDE names the danger. DREAD measures the danger. PASTA is the seven-course meal that ties it all to the business.

question.prompt: During a design review of an online shop, the team notes that an attacker could change the price of an item in the message sent between the customer's browser and the server. Which STRIDE category BEST describes this threat?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
question.explanation: Changing data without permission is tampering, and it breaks integrity. Spoofing is tempting because attacks often involve fake identity, but here the attacker changes data and does not pretend to be anyone.

topics.name: Supply chain risk management
topics.simpleExplanation: A supply chain is every company and step involved in giving you a product or service. If any link is weak, you can be harmed. A restaurant can serve bad food because a supplier sent bad meat. In security, hardware may be faked or altered, software may carry hidden flaws, and service providers may be careless. Reduce the risk by assessing suppliers, watching them over time, setting minimum security requirements and agreeing service levels. Remember that your organization stays accountable for its data, even when someone else handles it.

studyNotes.heading: What can go wrong
studyNotes.body:
Supply chain risk management (SCRM) means finding and reducing risk from the companies you buy from, and from the companies they buy from.

Risks by type:

Hardware

- Tampering: someone changes a product before it reaches you.
- Counterfeits: fake parts sold as real ones. They may fail early or hide bad features.
- Implants: hidden chips or code added to equipment.

Software

- Malicious code added during the build or an update.
- Vulnerable open source parts inside a product.

Services

- A cloud or support provider with weak security, poor recovery or staff with too much access.
- A provider that uses other subcontractors you do not know about.

Think of the question: who touched this before it reached me?

studyNotes.heading: Assessing and monitoring third parties
studyNotes.body:
A third party is an outside company you work with. Assess it before you sign, and keep checking afterwards.

Ways to assess:

- Questionnaires about its security.
- Reviewing audit reports, such as a System and Organization Controls (SOC) report, or an ISO 27001 certificate from the International Organization for Standardization.
- On-site audits or tests, where the contract allows.

Monitoring means continuing to check. A supplier that was safe last year may not be safe today. Watch for news of breaches, changes of ownership and missed service levels.

Buy from trusted sources and authorized resellers. Check the packaging and the product when it arrives.

studyNotes.heading: Minimum requirements and service levels
studyNotes.body:
Minimum security requirements are the lowest level of security a supplier must meet to do business with you. Put them in the contract. Include the right to audit and a duty to report breaches quickly. Flow them down to subcontractors.

A Service Level Requirement (SLR) describes what the customer needs. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is the formal promise from the provider, often with penalties if it is missed. Typical measures are uptime, response time and repair time.

Example: a shop needs its payment service up 99.9 percent of the time. That is its SLR. The contract then says the provider will meet 99.9 percent or pay a credit. That is the SLA.

studyNotes.heading: Technical protections
studyNotes.body:
A silicon root of trust is a security function built into a chip. It starts first and checks that the rest of the device's software is genuine and unchanged.

A physically unclonable function (PUF) uses tiny, natural differences made in each chip during manufacture. These work like a fingerprint and are extremely hard to copy.

A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a list of all the parts inside a piece of software, like the ingredients on a food label. When a flaw is announced in a common part, an SBOM tells you quickly whether you are affected.

studyNotes.heading: The management view
studyNotes.body: You can outsource the work, but you cannot outsource accountability. Involve procurement, legal and security staff from the start of any purchase. Plan what happens if a supplier fails or is breached.

keyTerms.meaning: Supply Chain Risk Management: reducing risk from suppliers and their suppliers.
A fake product sold as genuine.
Hidden hardware or code added to a product.
Service Level Requirement: what the customer needs from a service.
Service Level Agreement: the formal promise from a provider, often with penalties.
A security function in a chip that checks the device starts with genuine software.
Physically Unclonable Function: a chip's natural, hard-to-copy fingerprint.
Software Bill of Materials: a list of all the parts inside software.

keyPoints: Assess suppliers before signing, and keep monitoring them after.
Hardware risks include tampering, counterfeits and implants.
An SLR is the need, and an SLA is the formal promise.
You can outsource work, but not accountability.
topics.memoryHook: Ask of every product: who touched this before it reached me?

question.prompt: A serious flaw is announced in a popular open source logging component. A company runs dozens of purchased applications and needs to learn quickly which ones contain this component. Which item would help MOST if it had been collected from vendors in advance?
options: The service level agreement for each application
A signed non-disclosure agreement with each vendor
A certificate of insurance from each vendor
A software bill of materials for each application
question.explanation: A software bill of materials lists the parts inside each application, so you can search it for the flawed component. A service level agreement is tempting, but it covers service promises and says nothing about what the software contains.

topics.name: Security awareness, education and training
topics.simpleExplanation: People make many of the mistakes that attackers rely on, so an organization must teach them. Awareness reminds everyone what to watch for. Training teaches the skills a person needs for a job. Education builds deep understanding, usually for security staff. A good program uses methods people actually remember, such as practice phishing emails, games and friendly security champions. Content must be reviewed regularly, because attacks and technology keep changing. The program must also be measured, because attending a class does not prove that behaviour has changed.

studyNotes.heading: Awareness, training and education
studyNotes.body:
These three words are not the same.

- Awareness: makes people notice security. It is for everyone. Posters, short videos and reminders are examples. It answers what.
- Training: teaches a specific skill for a job. A help desk worker learns how to check a caller's identity. It answers how.
- Education: builds deep knowledge and understanding over a longer time, such as a degree or a professional certification. It answers why.

A school example: a sign reminding children to wash their hands is awareness. Teaching the kitchen staff to handle food safely is training. A university course on food science is education.

The program needs senior management support, and it should suit each audience. A cleaner, a payroll clerk and a programmer face different risks.

studyNotes.heading: Methods and techniques
studyNotes.body:
Social engineering means tricking people into giving away information or access. Teach staff the warning signs: urgency, fear, unusual requests and secrecy. Teach them to check a request using a second, trusted route, such as calling a known phone number.

Phishing is a fake message designed to trick someone. Spear phishing targets a particular person or group. Whaling targets senior leaders. Vishing uses voice calls, and smishing uses text messages. Simulated phishing means sending safe practice emails. A person who clicks gets quick, kind teaching and not punishment. Punishment makes people hide their mistakes.

Security champions are staff in ordinary departments who volunteer to promote good security and bring questions forward. They carry the message closer to daily work.

Gamification means using games, points and friendly contests to make learning stick. A department that reports the most phishing attempts could win a prize.

Make reporting easy, and thank people for reporting.

studyNotes.heading: Periodic content reviews
studyNotes.body:
A course that never changes soon becomes out of date. Review content on a regular schedule and after any major incident or change. Include emerging technology and trends:

- Artificial intelligence: computer systems that can write convincing messages or copy a voice, making scams harder to spot.
- Cryptocurrency: digital money, often demanded by criminals because payments are hard to reverse.
- Blockchain: a shared digital record that is very hard to change.

Review also means removing old material. Keep it short, relevant and matched to real incidents seen by the organization.

studyNotes.heading: Measuring effectiveness
studyNotes.body:
Attendance only tells you who was present. It does not tell you what changed. Better measures show changes in behaviour.

Good measures:

- Fewer people clicking on simulated phishing emails.
- More people reporting suspicious messages, and reporting them sooner.
- Fewer incidents caused by human error.
- Better results on tests before and after training.

Worked example: in January, 30 of 200 staff click a practice phishing email, which is 15 percent. In June, 10 of 200 click, which is 5 percent. Reports rise from 20 to 90. This shows that behaviour has improved. Share such results with management, and use them to improve the program.

keyTerms.meaning: Keeping everyone alert to security issues.
Teaching a specific skill needed for a job.
Building deep understanding over a longer time.
Tricking people into giving information or access.
A fake message designed to trick someone.
Safe practice emails used to test and teach staff.
A staff member in a department who promotes good security.
Using games and points to make learning stick.

keyPoints: Awareness is what, training is how, and education is why.
Match content to each audience and role.
Review content regularly to include new threats and technology.
Measure changes in behaviour, not only attendance.
topics.memoryHook: Awareness opens the eyes. Training trains the hands. Education fills the head.

question.prompt: A caller used a computer-generated copy of the finance director's voice to trick a help desk worker into resetting an account. The company's security course has not changed for three years. What is the BEST long-term action for the awareness program?
options: Set a regular content review that adds emerging threats and real incidents
Dismiss the help desk worker to show that mistakes carry a penalty
Make the existing course twice as long and hold it every month
Ask all staff to sign the current security policy once more
question.explanation: The cause is out-of-date content, so regular reviews that include new threats fix the root problem. Repeating the same course more often is tempting, but it still would not teach about voice cloning.

examQuestions.prompt: You hold the CISSP and discover that a fellow certified member lied about work experience to gain the certification. You have clear evidence. What should you do?
options: Post the evidence on a professional networking site as a warning
Say nothing, because it does not affect your employer
Tell the person's employer and ask for the person to be dismissed
Submit a formal complaint with the evidence to ISC2
examQuestions.explanation: Fraud in certification harms the profession, and a fellow professional may complain under Canon 4 through the formal process. Telling the employer is tempting, but it skips the correct process and is not your decision to force.

examQuestions.prompt: A data centre is worth $400,000. A power surge would damage 25 percent of it and is expected once every two years. A protection system would cost $20,000 a year and would reduce the expected rate to once every ten years. Based only on this information, what should the security manager recommend?
options: Buy it, because its yearly value is $20,000
Do not buy it, because it costs $10,000 more than it saves
Buy it, because its yearly value is $40,000
Do not buy it, because the annual loss would not change
examQuestions.explanation: SLE is $400,000 x 0.25 = $100,000. ALE before is $100,000 x 0.5 = $50,000, and ALE after is $100,000 x 0.1 = $10,000. Value is $50,000 - $10,000 - $20,000 = $20,000. The $40,000 answer is tempting, but it forgets the cost of the safeguard.

examQuestions.prompt: A newly hired Chief Information Security Officer finds that departments ignore security rules, that no approved policy exists, and that each team buys its own tools. What should the new leader do FIRST?
options: Buy one central security product for every department
Obtain senior management support and an approved policy
Write detailed step-by-step procedures for each team to follow from now on
Begin disciplining staff who ignore the current rules
examQuestions.explanation: Governance works from the top down, so leadership support and an approved policy come first. Writing procedures is tempting, but procedures have no authority without a policy behind them.

examQuestions.prompt: A security analyst is helping human resources look into an employee's excessive personal web use. While reviewing the employee's work computer, the analyst finds records suggesting the employee has been stealing customer card numbers. What should the analyst do FIRST?
options: Ask the employee to explain the records in a private meeting
Finish the web use review and mention the records in the final report
Stop, preserve the evidence, and inform management and legal advisers
Copy the card numbers to a personal drive so that they are safe
examQuestions.explanation: An administrative case may now be criminal, so evidence must be protected and the right people told. Questioning the employee is tempting, but it may warn the suspect and damage the case.

examQuestions.prompt: A business impact analysis finds that an insurance claims system has a Maximum Tolerable Downtime of 10 hours. After the system is restored, staff need 4 hours to test it and enter missed claims. What is the longest Recovery Time Objective that can be accepted?
options: 4 hours
10 hours
14 hours
6 hours
examQuestions.explanation: RTO plus work recovery time must not exceed MTD, so 10 - 4 = 6 hours. The 10 hour answer is tempting, but it leaves no time to test the system and catch up.

examQuestions.prompt: A European company wants to move customer records to a cloud provider that stores data in a country outside the European Union. The provider offers the lowest price. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Confirm a lawful transfer basis with legal advisers and agree contract terms
Sign the contract now to secure the price, then encrypt the data once it has been moved
Ask the provider's sales team to confirm that its service is safe
Move a small part of the customer records to test the service
examQuestions.explanation: Moving personal data across borders needs a lawful basis under GDPR, and supplier duties belong in the contract before any data moves. Encryption is tempting and useful, but it does not by itself settle the legal question, and a sales promise is not an assessment.

examQuestions.prompt: A bank wants a threat modeling method that links technical attacks to business impact. It wants to work through set stages, from defining business objectives to analyzing and managing risk. Which method BEST fits?
options: STRIDE
PASTA
DREAD
An attack tree
examQuestions.explanation: PASTA is a seven-stage, risk-centric method that begins with business objectives. STRIDE is tempting because it is widely known, but it classifies types of threat and is not a staged business risk process.

examQuestions.prompt: A company has run a security awareness program for a year and the chief executive asks whether it is working. Which measure gives the BEST evidence?
options: The percentage of staff who completed the online course
The number of posters displayed in the offices
Fewer clicks on practice phishing and more staff reports
The amount of money spent on the program during the year
examQuestions.explanation: Clicks and reports show a change in real behaviour. Completion percentage is tempting because it is easy to count, but it proves attendance and not learning.

examQuestions.prompt: A system administrator with wide access is to be dismissed this afternoon for serious misconduct. Human resources will hold the meeting at 3 p.m. When should the administrator's access be disabled?
options: At the end of the working day, after the person has gone home
Within 24 hours, once the signed termination papers are filed
At the same moment the person is told, or just before the meeting
One week before the meeting, so that nothing can go wrong
examQuestions.explanation: Timing access removal with the meeting stops any harmful action and avoids giving warning. Disabling a week early is tempting, but it would alert the person and interrupt normal work.

examQuestions.prompt: A hospital plans to add a strict login step that could delay nurses and doctors from opening patient records during emergencies. The privacy team strongly supports the change. What should the security adviser recommend?
options: Apply the strict login everywhere, because confidentiality of records is a legal duty
Design access with an audited emergency route, so that care is not delayed and use is reviewed
Remove login controls in emergency departments so that care is never slowed
Postpone any decision until the next external audit gives its opinion
examQuestions.explanation: Safety comes first, and security should fit the mission of the hospital. An emergency route with review keeps care moving and keeps accountability. Removing all controls is tempting, but it gives up confidentiality and nonrepudiation when they can be kept.
